summary: Answer quickly, then process slow work in the background without losing jobs.
goals: Why slow work should happen outside a user request
How producers, queues, and consumers work together
How acknowledgements, retries, and dead-letter queues work
How to keep order and apply backpressure

steps.title: Slow work blocks the request
body: Creators upload videos. Each upload needs about 30 seconds of work to convert it into several sizes. Right now the web server does that work before answering the upload request. The creator waits, requests time out, and video processing slows down other pages too.
steps.callout: Slow, heavy, or unreliable work inside a request—such as video conversion, email, reports, or a third-party call—makes the user wait.

steps.title: Put a queue between the request and the work
body: The web server saves the upload, puts a small job message on a message queue, then replies: “processing—we’ll notify you.” Separate worker machines take jobs from the queue and convert the videos. The web server is the producer; the workers are consumers.
steps.callout: Popular options include RabbitMQ, Amazon SQS, Google Pub/Sub, and Kafka, a retained event log that can also be used as a queue.

steps.title: Let a queue absorb a spike
body: A popular creator goes live and uploads increase tenfold. Without a queue, the spike could overload the web servers. With a queue, web servers stay quick because they only add jobs. The jobs wait in line while workers continue at a steady pace, then catch up after the rush.
steps.callout: A queue turns “too much work right now” into “some users wait longer for the result.” This is called load leveling.

steps.title: Add workers to catch up faster
body: To finish the backlog sooner, start more workers. Each job goes to one worker, not all of them. This is the competing consumers pattern. Workers can be added easily because they are stateless. Teams may automatically add workers when the queue grows.
steps.callout: Scale producers and consumers separately: add web servers for more requests and workers for more processing.

steps.title: A worker can fail before it finishes
body: A worker crashes halfway through a video. If the queue deleted the job as soon as it handed it out, the work would be lost and the creator might wait forever. Workers can crash or be replaced, so the queue must allow for failures.
steps.callout: Handing a job to a worker does not mean the worker has finished it.

steps.title: Acknowledge only after finishing
body: Keep a job hidden while a worker is processing it. When the work is done, the worker sends an acknowledgement (ack), and the queue deletes the job. If no ack arrives before a timeout, the job appears again for another worker. This means a job may run twice—for example, if a worker finishes but crashes before sending its ack. Make jobs idempotent, so repeating one does not change the result twice.
steps.callout: This is at-least-once delivery: a job is retried until acknowledged, but duplicates are possible. Exactly-once behavior is difficult; idempotent workers help produce the same result.

steps.title: Move repeated failures aside
body: One upload is corrupt, so every worker that tries it fails. The queue retries the same job again and again, using workers and blocking other work. Count attempts and move a job to a dead-letter queue (DLQ) after, for example, three failures. A person or script can inspect it there.
steps.callout: Alert when the dead-letter queue grows. It can be an early sign of a bug or bad input.

steps.title: Events may finish out of order
body: An account has events named created, email changed, and deleted. Several workers process them in parallel. A slow worker may finish “email changed” after another worker has already handled “deleted.” Many queues do not promise order, and parallel workers can change completion order even if messages were read in order.
steps.callout: If correctness depends on order, design and enforce that order explicitly.

steps.title: Keep order per key with partitions
body: Systems such as Kafka divide a topic into partitions. Messages with the same key, such as an account ID, go to the same partition. One worker reads each partition in order. Events for one account stay in order, while different accounts can be handled in parallel by other partitions.
steps.callout: Order is guaranteed per key, not across every message. Global order usually means one consumer and no parallel processing.

steps.title: A queue cannot create more capacity
body: A queue can absorb a spike, but if jobs arrive faster than workers finish them for hours, the backlog keeps growing and can fill storage. Watch the age of the oldest job, not just the queue length. Add workers, cap the queue, or ask producers to slow down or reject new jobs with a clear “try later.”
steps.callout: A queue buys time; it does not add capacity. Over time, workers must process jobs at least as fast as they arrive.

steps.title: Recap
body:
• Move slow work out of the request: add a job to a queue and answer quickly.
  • Queues absorb spikes; add workers to reduce the backlog.
  • Acknowledge after work is done. Retries can create duplicates, so make jobs idempotent.
  • Move repeatedly failing jobs to a dead-letter queue.
  • Use partitions to keep order per key, watch queue age, and push back when needed.
